chapter: Young players, Coltrane and the avant-garde
title: New Orleans musical families, New York backbiting and Lockjaw's jam sessions
summary: Sam says New Orleans players learn from fathers, and recalls Eddie Lockjaw Davis publicly correcting weak players as a lesson.

story.theme_name: Coming to New York: clubs, jams, and making it
story.community_name: Making it in New York: arrival, clubs and the scene

blocks.x: But, you see, you find those guys, well, it's a common thing in New Orleans, man, don't you see, because, uh, their fathers were fine musicians and their father was a teacher and they send them to--after they come home from a teacher their father teaches, you see, so that makes them fine musicians down there. But you see, those folks, man, they don't ever leave, see they stay, stay down there man. You know, because, uh,--

But you know the thing that I've always felt too, saying one of the things that that happened right here in New York it seems to me-I mean this is just my perception of it--I don't know how you feel about it. But, Slide Hampton and I was talking about this about a year ago, and Slide was saying, he said, one of the things that I really have...New York about is it cats are willing to tell a kid that that he sounds good and then turn him around behind his back and talk about him like a dog. Why don't the cat just walk up to him-a cat, I mean if you really are committed and you got love, you know for the love of my piece like he used to say, for the love of it--if that's the way you really feel about what's happening, why don't you just tell the cat, hey, man, you sound good but why don't you try this or do something like this, you know, or whatever, you know. And then help a cat out rather than...then the next thing you know a dude walk around with an attitude and

everybody say look at that jive motherfucker, you know, he's--who does he think he is. And there's all kinds of --these cats get into those kind of little bags, you know. Whereas...jam session used to be going on like if you got up on the stage and your shit wasn't correct the cat would tell you, I mean, very harshly, and might even kick your ass--

That's right. I remember--those things aren't happening anymore. I remember some sessions, man, I used to be where uh, uh,Eddie... not Cleanheadwhat am I talking about, uh Lockjaw--used to be playing and he with a cold, some guys, you know, somebody want to play and he get up on the stand and Lockjaw would read it, man, if he mess up, right there before everybody, man, why would you get up here if you know you couldn't handle this, you know, see. Now you come up here and embarass yourself, you know, and embarass us, embarass-- I remember a drummer, got up there one time, man, and and Lockjaw was playing one of those swift numbers and the man couldn't, he couldn't keep up, Lockjaw stopped the song, man, and read it right there before everybody, you know. He said...you shouldn't got up here in the first place. So, but I mean he wasn't doing it to hurt his feelings, you see, he was doing it as a lesson man, you see.
